title: All mine is with me
hook: Stilpo lost city, wife and children and said everything of his was still with him

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Democritus, for whom one listener counted as a whole people. Your line was one is enough.

A city has just fallen. The conqueror, a king called Demetrius, nicknamed the Besieger of Cities, has taken Megara. Houses are wrecked, goods carried off, families scattered. Somewhere in the ruins stands a philosopher named Stilpo, whose home is gone and whose wife and children are lost to him. The king asks him: have you lost anything? Seneca tells the story, and Stilpo's answer, in his ninth letter.
screen: `MEGARA HAS FALLEN.` → `HAVE YOU LOST ANYTHING?` → `ALL MINE IS WITH ME.`

segments.voice: Stilpo told the king: I have all my goods with me. He meant his true goods, Seneca explains, the kind no hand can seize. What was scattered, wrecked and carried off he didn't count as his own, only as things that had come to him from outside. It's fair to flinch at this. Losing a family is not a small thing, and Seneca doesn't say it is. In the same letter he says the wise person feels their troubles, and then overcomes them. Not numb. Not untouched. Still standing. The surprise is where Seneca puts the story: in a letter about friendship. Lucilius has asked whether someone complete in themselves needs friends at all. Seneca says the wise person is content with themselves, and can live without friends if they must, but still wants them, very much. Not to have someone who'll sit at their bedside, but to have someone at whose bedside they can sit. So Stilpo's line isn't a reason to love less. Read this way, it's a reason to love without fear. If what's most yours can't be taken, you can give your heart to people and things freely, knowing that even if you lose them, you won't lose yourself. In Seneca's Latin: omnia mea mecum sunt. All mine is with me.
screen: `I HAVE ALL MY GOODS WITH ME.` · `FEELING IT, AND STILL STANDING.` · `WANTING FRIENDS ANYWAY.` · `LOVE WITHOUT FEAR.` · then, large: `ALL MINE IS WITH ME.`

segments.voice: Count on your fingers a few things that are yours in Stilpo's sense, things no fire, thief or bad day could take: your honesty, your patience on good days, what you've learned, the love you give. Name three, slowly. Then rest your hands together in your lap, as if holding them.
Stilpo. The philosopher in fallen Megara who told the king: I have all my goods with me, the kind no hand can seize.
Your line: you won't lose yourself. What's most yours stays with you. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism reflect on which of their goods are truly their own, character, judgment, kindness, so that losses elsewhere do not take away their footing.

notes: Review (2026-10-01): SERIOUS fix: the list 'justice, courage, good sense' comes from De Constantia 5.6, not Letter 9; teach, word, match, fork and trapdoor now follow Letter 9.18–19 (true goods no hand can seize; what was plundered counted as from outside). Cut 'two thousand years', 'stuck for centuries as a proverb', 'old', 'smoke' and the proverb myth.

Letter 9.18–19: Demetrius Poliorcetes takes Megara; Stilpo, having lost his children and wife, answers 'omnia mea mecum sunt'; Seneca glosses his goods as justice, virtue, temperance, prudence. Paraphrased; confirm the list of virtues.
Letter 9.3: the wise man 'feels' his troubles but overcomes them; 9.8: the wise man wants a friend in order to have someone by whose sickbed he can sit. Paraphrased; confirm.
Whether Stilpo's family were killed or captured is not specified by Seneca ('lost'); the script keeps 'lost to him'.
Zeno studying with Stilpo (Diogenes Laertius 7.2, 7.24) and Cicero's 'omnia mecum porto mea' attributed to Bias (Paradoxa Stoicorum 1.8): confirm.
